analysis.one_liner: Gives Americans rights over their personal data and creates a new federal privacy agency to enforce them.
analysis.headline: Introduced March 19, 2026 with no cosponsors, and referred to three House committees, where it has not moved since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would give people legal rights over the personal information companies collect about them online: the right to see it, correct it, delete it, and take it with them, plus the right to a human review of decisions made about them by algorithms. Companies would need clear consent before running targeted personalization or selling data, deceptive consent screens ('dark patterns') would be banned, and a new Digital Privacy Agency would enforce the rules, backed by state attorneys general and private lawsuits. It also creates a new federal crime for 'doxxing' — publishing someone's personal information to intimidate or incite violence against them. As of now it has been referred to three committees and has no cosponsors.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses the internet. The bill defines personal information broadly as any data linked or reasonably linkable to a person or device, so the rights and protections reach essentially all Americans. People gain the ability to find out what data companies hold, who they sold it to, demand deletion, opt out of behavioral profiling used for targeted advertising, get human review of automated decisions affecting things like credit or hiring, sue for violations, and avoid forced arbitration of privacy claims. Domestic-abuse and stalking victims would gain a new criminal tool against doxxers.

how_it_helps.text: Creates enforceable rights of access, correction, deletion, and portability: individuals can see what personal information a company holds and who it has been shared with, demand corrections or deletion, and move their data to a competing service through a publicly documented interface, with no fees for routine requests.

Requires express, affirmative consent before a company uses personal information for behavioral personalization (algorithmic targeting or content shaping) and again annually, and bans 'dark patterns' that trick people into giving consent or obscure privacy policies.

Establishes a Digital Privacy Agency with investigative and litigation powers, an Office of Civil Rights, and a complaint process; enforcement is layered with state attorneys general and private rights of action, and agreements to waive the law's protections or force privacy claims into predispute arbitration are void.

Bars companies from processing personal information to discriminate in jobs, credit, insurance, housing, or education based on race, religion, sex, disability, and other protected classes, and directs the agency to write disparate-impact rules.
Makes it a federal crime punishable by up to 5 years to publish someone's personal information with intent to threaten, intimidate, harass, or incite violence against them (doxxing).

Requires companies to minimize the data they collect, keep records of employee access to sensitive data, notify people of breaches and data-sharing abuse, protect end-to-end encryption, and prohibits re-identification of de-identified data.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers, ad-tech companies, and large online platforms whose business models depend on collecting, profiling, and sharing personal information. They would need consent for profiling and disclosure, could collect only what a service reasonably needs, could not link advertising identifiers across sites, and would face compliance costs, audits, and potential penalties. Consumers could also see some ad-supported 'free' services change, since less profiling means less targeted-advertising revenue. Some smaller online businesses face obligations too: any commercial activity above $5,000 in revenue or 5,000 people's data counts, though businesses under $25 million in revenue with under 200 employees are exempt from many of the heaviest requirements.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs are real. Even with exemptions for small businesses, firms must build consent systems, deletion and portability infrastructure, and API access, and the definition of a covered entity is broad (over $5,000 revenue or 5,000 individuals' data), pulling many modest businesses into scope.

The consent-and-minimization model could reduce the revenue that funds free ad-supported services, and the bill does not ban charging people different prices for privacy, so some feared a two-tier system where only those who can afford it get real privacy.

The new doxxing crime raises free-speech concerns; the bill includes a journalism carve-out for coverage of public officials and matters of public interest, but a criminal speech offense of this breadth would draw First Amendment challenge.

Creating and staffing a new federal agency is a permanent cost to taxpayers, and the Director is given wide rulemaking discretion over consent thresholds, exemptions, and disparate-impact standards, which concentrates significant power in one appointed official.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the benefit is large: the United States currently has no comprehensive federal privacy law, so these rights would be new. The costs fall mainly on the industries that monetize data, with some spillover onto consumers through ad-supported services and onto taxpayers for the new agency. The bill is carefully drafted — layered enforcement, small-business ramp-ups, security and fraud exemptions — but its breadth and its ban on forced arbitration of privacy claims guarantee a long legal fight. On balance the consumer protections outweigh the compliance costs; the practical weakness is not the design but the lack of any political support on record.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to three House committees in March 2026, and nothing has happened since — no cosponsors, no hearing, no vote — while the Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Zoe Lofgren introduced the Online Privacy Act of 2026 in the House on March 19, 2026.
The same day, the bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, and Science, Space, and Technology committees; no committee has taken it up since.
The bill has zero cosponsors, so no other member has publicly backed it so far.
The bill text creates individual data rights, company obligations, a new Digital Privacy Agency, enforcement by state attorneys general and private lawsuits, and a new criminal doxxing offense.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet. For now the status quo holds: data brokers, ad-tech firms, and large platforms continue to collect and sell personal information under no comprehensive federal privacy law, and internet users still have none of the rights this bill would create.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and platforms, for now

for.name: Zoe Lofgren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Online Privacy Act of 2026 and referred it to three House committees.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has one Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no votes or public opposition on record, so no partisan shape has emerged yet.

industries.note: These companies buy, sell, and profile personal information for advertising. The bill requires named-party consent for sales, bans collecting more than a service reasonably needs, and bars linking identifiers across ad disclosures — dismantling the core of their business model, which profits by tracking people who never meaningfully agreed to it.

industries.industry: Large online platforms and social media
industries.note: Platforms would need annual express consent for behavioral personalization, could lose the ability to condition service on profiling, and must delete data on request — costs to their engagement and advertising models. On the other hand, a single national rulebook with safe harbors for approved consent processes could be easier to manage than today's patchwork of state laws.

Businesses under $25 million in revenue with fewer than 200 employees are exempt from many major provisions and get a nine-month ramp-up when they outgrow the exemption, shielding startups — though the covered-entity threshold still reaches commercial activity above $5,000 in revenue.
The bill bars companies from preventing users from using encryption and gives legal recognition to privacy-preserving computing as a compliance path, expanding demand for these tools.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to three committees with no cosponsors almost never reach the floor. The sponsor's previous versions of this same bill in earlier Congresses likewise never received a vote, and comprehensive federal privacy legislation has repeatedly stalled in committee over disputes about state-law preemption and private lawsuits. Absent cosponsors or a committee hearing in the coming months, the likeliest path is that this bill sits until the Congress ends in January 2027.
